newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania pulls back from brink, but future murky.
newsitem.headline: Albania pulls back from brink, but future murky.

text.p: Albania appears to have pulled back from the brink of total meltdown, but huge problems remain as this tiny Balkan country struggles to end the anarchy threatening to tear it apart.
At one point last week the country seemed to be slipping into the abyss after civilians emptied arms depots vacated by demoralised soldiers and gun law prevailed as police melted away.

Unlike an armed rebellion that broke out in the south of the country last month against the government over failed pyramid savings schemes, the rush to arms in the north appeared to be motivated mainly by a perceived need for self-protection.

A new all-party government sworn in last week appears to have restored some sort of order in the capital by raising police wages by 300 per cent and creating special units on even higher pay to disarm the gunmen.

As the government organised a ceremony on Sunday to mourn more than 100 people killed in Albania during the violence, most by falling bullets in several days of almost continuous random firing, an edgy calm descended on the capital.

But beyond the immediate security situation the future looked decidedly uncertain with the south still in rebel hands, a Kalashnikov stored in every home, food running out and the West divided on whether or not to intervene.

At the centre of the crisis is President Sali Berisha. The rebels are insisting he step down, blaming him for allowing the shady schemes that collapsed with the life savings of thousands, before they hand back their weapons.
But despite growing international pressure on him to go, the right-wing president first elected in 1992 insists on staying on until new elections by June.
Western diplomats in Tirana who have met the beleaguered Albanian leader regularly over the past few weeks say he had given no indication that he was ready to step down.

Berisha has pledged to stand down if his Democratic Party, which won a landslide in elections last year condemned by the opposition and international observers as unfair, is beaten. He would have to go anyway in this case, since parliament elects the president.
Some opposition politicians fear however that with the key Interior Ministry handling police and local councils in Democrat hands, the possibility of manipulation still exists.

They want a large presence of international monitors under the authority of the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), many more than the 500 or so deployed at the last poll which was branded as seriously flawed.

While the OSCE has already offered to help in the elections, the response to demands by both the government and the rebels for European military peacekeepers to help disarm the gunmen have been coolly received.
Western officials argued that unlike in the Bosnian war, where peacekeepers went in after neighbouring nations intervened to seize territory, there is no war in Albania and no outside intervention.

Despite strong support for an international "stabilisation" force from European mediator Franz Vranitzky, the former Austrian leader, most Western governments said such a force was out of the question at present.
"To say you are going to occupy the country doesn't make sense," said a senior U.S. official who declined to be named.

This raised the prospect of a political and security stalemate with rebels insisting on surrendering weapons only to international peacekeepers and the international community saying it will not come in until the rebellion is ended.
Some Western leaders argue that some sort of international force will be needed soon, if only to secure the airport and the anarchic port of Durres to enable humanitarian aid to be sent in.

Looting and panic buying combined with lawlessness on the main routes leading to neighbouring countries has meant that supplies of food are running low, with prices for some staples doubling in the past few days.

There could also be a downside for the government in its high-risk strategy of encouraging new police recruits with high pay and the allocation of a gun, with some critics saying it is handing arms to those who missed out in the looting.
But with thousands of arms already in private hands, and the price of a Kalashnikov automatic rifle just $3 on the streets of Tirana, the government clearly thinks it is a risk worth taking.
